extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improvisation coaches, drama teachers and workshop leaders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for coaching and performing short-form improvisational storytelling (especially the 'What Comes Next' game): building platforms, accepting offers, breaking routines, keeping promises to the audience, and diagnosing group weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yes, and / accepting offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn to accept ideas without fear, embrace the possibilities that other people’s ideas open up, and you will discover that people are drawn to this positivity. Adopt the procedure yourself and (with a little practice) you can make almost anyone treat you as a friend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting an offer develops it, continues it, pushes it into the future. Teach beginners to accept rather than block; acceptance builds a platform and allows scenes to progress. Examples: respond to a dangerous-moment offer by treating it as real and building on the danger rather than denying it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking as killing an idea
rubrics_metrics.description: A block is killing an idea, denying the audience something they thought they had been promised. The distinction is not dependent on the words 'yes' and 'no.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blocking denies promised storylines and robs the audience. Example anti-pattern: turning a dangerous offer into a benign item (e.g., treating a mime gun robbery as a watch exchange) which removes the promised stakes. Coaches should correct trivial blocks for beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fear-based blocks from confident blocking
rubrics_metrics.description: One question a coach has to consider is whether an apparent block is made out of fear or out of confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inexperienced improvisers block out of fear (e.g., insisting on tea when coffee is offered), correct them. If experienced improvisers block for character choice or playfulness, allow it. Teach blocking deliberately only later; early emphasis should be on accepting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do only what you're asked (game rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 'What Comes Next' the volunteer must do what the audience tells them and only what they’re told—don’t embellish!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The game is theoretical: the actor should avoid embellishing since that influences the audience's suggestions and obscures which ideas came from whom. Use a visible actor to remove ambiguity; ask additional actors to play new characters when needed to visualize suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a platform before introducing trouble
rubrics_metrics.description: The group learns to build one story idea on another, to create a PLATFORM rather than plunging the hero into disaster straight away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A platform shows the hero and what 'normal' looks like so the audience cares when trouble arrives. Platforms can be short or long depending on story length and audience familiarity; specific, rich detail in the platform (names, props, habits) increases audience investment and generates 'obvious' next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be obvious / use 'the next obvious idea'
rubrics_metrics.description: Remind them of Yes And and encourage them to yes and each other’s ideas. You might also use the phrase 'The next obvious idea.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness prevents scenes from lurching off-topic and makes choices easier. Encourage specificity (e.g., naming who 'someone' is) so subsequent offers become 'obvious' and 'right.' Obvious doesn't mean dull if the detail is interesting and motivating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vagueness and 'wimp' offers
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'someone' here is a dead giveaway. This a wimp, a failure to define.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague offers (someone, nobody) stop the story from having direction. Encourage defining identities and relationships early to change how subsequent events play out (e.g., sister vs policeman changes stakes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canceling (undoing previous offers) is harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Canceling undoes the effect of the previous offer: a cousin of blocking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: positive idea immediately negated by a negative idea (fire then rain) prevents development. Coach groups to make consecutive ideas move the story forward rather than cancel each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break routines in ways that provide point
rubrics_metrics.description: Interrupting or breaking a routine must retrospectively provide the point of the action; arbitrary breaks feel pointless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good breaks exploit latent promises in the routine (milking cow → cow says 'I love the way you do that'), bad breaks are arbitrary (alien spaceship that is irrelevant). When breaking a routine, make the break relevant to what was established or provide justification to reconnect it to the platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary originality / arbitrary absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Unnecessary originality crops up ... improvisers simply don’t believe that obviousness is a virtue and work hard to show off how imaginative they are. But being arbitrary is trivial and ... has little to do with keeping a story on the rails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absurd juxtapositions must be justified by the platform; otherwise they fail to inspire others (example: rat-and-marshmallow stew). Use originality when it pays off promises or raises stakes, not merely to stand out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep promises to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience is constantly one step ahead of you... What you give them will either be better than what they expected or not as good as what they expected... Most of the time it will not be as good as what they expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial offers create promises (e.g., trip to Grandma). Either deliver what's promised (without delay) or substitute a better payoff that still honors the general promise. Breaking promised expectations without payoff turns the audience off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform length must suit story length and familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: A platform should be sustained until just before it gets boring... platform length varies according to how long the story is and how familiar the platform is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer platforms support longer stories; familiar settings allow shorter platforms (assume audience knowledge). Use the platform to make later trouble meaningful (examples: Die Hard III vs Fellowship of the Ring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use feedback (yay/boo) to calibrate audience taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Coach the group to shout 'Yay!' for suggestions they like and 'Boo!' for those they dislike. A majority of boos means that you will give them another chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach groups to give honest feedback quickly; this accustoms improvisers to low-stakes failure and helps them learn. As coach, interpret audience instinct rather than imposing abstract rules; ask why the group booed to find a rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bridging (delaying obvious action without purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bridging: substituting the obvious action with an original action to delay completion (and so spin out the scene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bridging often produces endless small steps that lead nowhere. Use deliberate suspense if justified, but avoid wheel-spinning that prevents the story from moving into the next phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right trouble for the right hero
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'obvious' trouble is 'right' for a given hero. Certain platforms promise certain kinds of trouble, and good improvisers, improvisers happy to be obvious, deliver that kind of trouble—and then look for ways to make it worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match trouble to who the hero is and the promises of the platform. Avoid 'trouble salad'—multiple unrelated trouble sources that dilute focus. Once the right trouble is found, develop it instead of adding unrelated complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reincorporate ideas to provide structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The group learns to build one story idea on another ... to reincorporate ideas to provide structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring earlier details back later to create payoff and cohesion (reusing names, props, lines). This creates structure and makes later developments feel earned rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage ensemble support and quick role-playing
rubrics_metrics.description: Depending on the size (and mood) of the group, I may ask that as and when extra characters are created, additional actors jump up to play them. This also instills the virtue of jumping up to support your fellow improvisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote quick willingness to play added characters; supports clarity and shared ownership of the scene. Use these jumps to visualize audience suggestions and reduce ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the game to diagnose weaknesses and adapt teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: This theoretical game is an excellent way of teaching key storytelling concepts to a new group, as well as diagnosing weaknesses in a more experienced group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the game may be too theoretical for children or teenagers; adjust or simplify. When a group repeatedly fails in a pattern (e.g., wimping, canceling, arbitrary originality), address one remedy at a time and make mental notes for later coaching.
